opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that one surprised us at first, honestly. The intuition most people carry around is that you want your auto-labels to be as clean as possible, so you crank the confidence threshold up and only keep the detections the foundation model is really sure about. Precision feels safe.

But what we saw was that when you lower the threshold, somewhere in the range of 0.2 or 0.3 rather than 0.5 or higher, the downstream detector you train on those labels actually performs better. The way I interpret it is that recall matters more than we tend to give it credit for in this setting. With a high threshold you throw away a lot of true objects, especially the harder ones: small objects, occluded objects, unusual viewpoints, things the zero-shot model is a little less certain about. Those are exactly the examples the downstream model needs to learn from. If they're missing, the model learns that those regions are background, which is a really damaging signal.

When you lower the threshold you let in some false positives, but deep detectors seem fairly robust to a moderate amount of that kind of noise. A spurious box here and there gets averaged out over a large dataset. Systematically missing whole categories of hard positives doesn't get averaged out. It biases the model.

So the takeaway for practitioners is that the auto-labeling threshold isn't just about label quality in isolation. It's a hyperparameter of the whole pipeline, and you should tune it for downstream performance, not for how clean the labels look when you inspect them. It also reframes where human effort should go. Rather than having people label everything from scratch, you can lean toward higher recall from the auto-labeler and spend human time reviewing and cleaning up, which is a much cheaper operation. That's a big part of why we think auto-labeling can get you most of the way there at a fraction of the cost.

r001.rationale: The candidate says lower thresholds improve downstream performance and that detectors tolerate moderate false-positive noise. It attributes the gain to retaining hard positives, though, and does not communicate that an appropriate amount of training noise itself can improve performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this one surprised a lot of people, including some folks on our team at first. The intuition most people have is that if you're going to use a model to generate labels for you, you want to be really conservative. Only keep the boxes the model is really sure about, because otherwise you're feeding noise back into training. And that intuition is just wrong, or at least incomplete.

The way I think about it is that there are two kinds of error you're trading off. When you set a high threshold, you get very precise labels, but you miss a huge number of true objects. And in a detection setting, a missed object isn't neutral. It becomes a negative. The detector you're training sees a region that clearly contains a car or a pedestrian, and the label is telling it, no, that's background. So a high threshold is actively teaching the model to suppress real objects. That's a systematic bias, and it's much more damaging than the random-ish noise you get from a few spurious boxes.

When you lower the threshold, yes, you let in some false positives. But a lot of those low-confidence detections are actually correct. They're the small objects, the occluded ones, the ones at the edge of the frame, the ones in unusual lighting. Those are exactly the hard cases a detector needs to see more of. So you're recovering recall on the long tail, and the training process is fairly robust to a modest amount of label noise as long as it isn't biased in one direction.

The other piece is that the confidence score isn't really calibrated in the way people assume. A 0.3 doesn't mean a 30 percent chance it's real. It often just means the model has less evidence, not that the evidence points the other way. So treating the threshold as a hard truth cutoff was never well founded to begin with.

I'd say the takeaway isn't "always lower your threshold." It's that the right threshold is an empirical question about what the downstream model actually learns from, and people have been setting it based on what looks clean to a human reviewer rather than what produces a better detector. Those are different objectives. And honestly it's a nice reminder that the labels are a means to an end. The thing you care about is the model's behavior on real data, so that's what you should be measuring against.

r001.rationale: The response says the training process can tolerate modest label noise and explains the benefit of recovering missed objects, but it does not clearly state that an appropriate amount of training noise can itself improve performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that the value of an auto-label isn’t captured by its confidence score alone. When you set a very high threshold, you tend to keep the easy examples—the objects the model already recognizes well. You get cleaner labels, but you may lose a lot of useful variation.

Lowering that threshold lets more of those harder examples into training. You also introduce errors, so there’s a tradeoff, but the downstream detector may benefit more from the additional coverage than it suffers from the noise. And for object detection, leaving an object unlabeled can itself be a problem: you can end up treating a real object as background.

So I wouldn’t interpret this as saying lower thresholds are always better. I’d interpret it as saying that optimizing the precision of your auto-labels isn’t necessarily the same as optimizing the performance of the model you train with them.

r001.rationale: The response says added coverage may outweigh the harm from label noise, but it treats noise as a cost rather than communicating that an appropriate amount of training noise can improve performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that confidence and usefulness aren’t quite the same thing. If you set a very high threshold, you tend to keep the easy examples—the ones the model already handles well. Lowering that threshold gives the downstream detector more examples and potentially more diversity, including harder cases that would otherwise be excluded.

There’s a tradeoff, of course, because you’re also introducing more incorrect labels. But the result suggests that, within the range tested, the benefit of that additional coverage outweighs the cost of the noise. I wouldn’t interpret it as saying lower is always better. It says we should choose the threshold based on downstream detector performance, rather than assuming that the cleanest-looking set of auto-labels will produce the best model.

r001.rationale: The response says broader coverage outweighs the cost of additional label noise, treating noise as a downside rather than explaining that an appropriate amount of training noise can itself improve performance.
